Interviewer: Welcome to School Stage. Alya, how long have you been working with the drama club?
Alya: I joined two years ago, but I have helped manage performances only since September. At first, I was nervous about speaking to the actors.
Interviewer: What are you preparing now?
Alya: We are putting on a short comedy next Thursday. Twelve pupils are acting, and another five are working behind the stage.
Interviewer: Do you write all the scripts yourself?
Alya: No. Our English teacher helps us write them. I organise rehearsals and check that the microphones and lights are ready.
Interviewer: Has anything gone wrong?
Alya: Last week one microphone stopped working. Instead of cancelling rehearsal, we practised the scene without it until a replacement arrived.
Interviewer: How many people can watch the performance?
Alya: The school hall has room for about one hundred and fifty people. We have invited parents and younger students.
Interviewer: What do you enjoy most?
Alya: Watching everyone cooperate. We have learned that a successful show depends on the whole team, not just the actors.

Nasser had enjoyed listening to the school radio since he was young, but he had never imagined presenting a programme himself. One afternoon, his English teacher invited students to create a weekly show about local talents. Nasser volunteered to interview a young musician who played traditional Omani instruments.

The team had been preparing for two weeks when their guest became ill. Some pupils suggested cancelling the first episode, but Nasser thought they could interview the school's music teacher instead. She agreed, and the group wrote new questions about practising, performing and working with other musicians.

On the recording day, the microphone suddenly stopped working. Nasser felt disappointed because he had already spent the morning checking the script. His friend Mariam remembered a spare recorder kept in the library. They tested it and began again, although the sound was slightly different from what they had planned.

The finished programme included a short interview, a report about the upcoming school concert and a message inviting younger pupils to join the drama club. When the show was played at assembly, Nasser heard students discussing their favourite parts.

He realised that entertainment was not only about famous performers. It also gave ordinary people a chance to share their skills, listen to one another and feel part of a community. The team decided to produce another episode the following week.

Interviewer: Welcome to Nature Watch. Salim, why did your class visit the turtle reserve?
Salim: We wanted to understand how sea turtles are protected. Our teacher reminded us that bright lights and noise can disturb them.
Interviewer: What did you learn from the ranger?
Salim: She explained that turtles return to beaches to lay their eggs. If people leave plastic on the sand, young turtles may become trapped.
Interviewer: Did you see any turtles?
Salim: Yes, we watched two from a safe distance. We did not touch them or use a camera flash.
Interviewer: Was there a problem during the visit?
Salim: Some visitors had left empty bottles near a path. The ranger asked us to collect them while wearing gloves.
Interviewer: How can young people help after the trip?
Salim: We can use reusable bottles, tell others not to litter and support beach clean-ups. If we protect nesting areas, more turtles may reach the sea safely.
Interviewer: What would you tell someone planning a visit?
Salim: Follow the rules and stay quiet. Seeing animals in their natural habitat is exciting, but their safety is more important than our photographs.

During a school visit to a nature reserve, Huda noticed that the guides spent more time looking for signs of animals than trying to see the animals themselves. She had expected to photograph every creature, but the ranger explained that wildlife often hides when people approach too closely.

The group followed a marked path beside a shallow lake. Huda saw tracks in the soft sand and guessed that they belonged to a turtle. Her friend Rashid thought they might have been made by a bird. The ranger asked both pupils to examine the marks carefully. The tracks were wide and ended near a small pool, so they were probably left by a turtle.

Later, the pupils found a plastic bag tangled among the plants. They wanted to remove it immediately, but the ranger told them to check whether an animal was nearby first. After she made sure the area was safe, they collected the rubbish using gloves.

As the sun became hotter, the students moved to a shaded observation point. They watched several birds drinking without disturbing them. Huda realised that careful observation could teach them more than a hurried photograph.

Before leaving, the class discussed ways to protect the reserve. They agreed to bring reusable bottles on future visits and to remind visitors to stay on marked paths. Huda wrote in her notebook that if everyone followed the rules, the animals would have a better chance of living safely in their natural habitat.

Interviewer: Welcome to Travel Talk. Maha, where did your school group travel last month?
Maha: We went to Nizwa for a day trip. Our bus left the school at half past seven, and the journey was comfortable.
Interviewer: What had you planned to see?
Maha: We were going to visit the fort first, then walk around the traditional market. We also wanted to meet a local craftsperson.
Interviewer: Did everything happen as planned?
Maha: Not quite. The market was unusually crowded, so our guide suggested visiting the craft workshop before lunch instead.
Interviewer: Was that a disappointment?
Maha: No, because the craftsperson showed us how to make a small basket, and we asked lots of questions. We visited the market later when it was quieter.
Interviewer: What did you take with you?
Maha: Water, comfortable shoes and a notebook. I had forgotten my camera, but my friend shared her photographs with me.
Interviewer: What advice would you give to another school group?
Maha: Check opening times, leave enough time between activities and be ready to change your plans. You can still have an interesting journey even when something unexpected happens.

Last month, Rania and her family planned a weekend visit to a mountain village. Rania wanted to explore an old fort, while her younger brother hoped to see a waterfall. Their father checked the weather forecast and the opening times before they left home. He also made sure the car had enough fuel for the journey.

They set off early on Friday morning. After an hour, the family reached a village where they stopped to ask a local shopkeeper about the best route. The shopkeeper explained that one road had been closed for repairs and suggested a safer road through a nearby valley. He also reminded them to drive slowly because the bends were narrow.

By midday, they had reached the fort. Rania was disappointed to learn that the guided tour would not begin for another forty minutes. Instead of waiting outside in the sun, the family visited a small craft exhibition nearby. Rania watched an artist making colourful baskets and bought a postcard for her friend.

Later, the guide explained how people had used the fort to protect the village. From the upper courtyard, Rania could see the mountains and the winding road they had followed. Her brother took several photographs but decided not to visit the waterfall because it was getting late.

On their way home, Rania wrote a short travel diary. She realised that checking information and being flexible had helped her family enjoy the trip despite the unexpected road closure.
